mainTopic: The dispute between רב and שמואל over whether we follow רוב (the majority) in money matters, using the case of a goring ox and testing it against a משנה about a כתובה and a ברייתא about a sold slave.
overview: The amud continues the argument between רב and שמואל about someone who bought an ox that turned out to gore, so it is useless for plowing. The גמרא first asks when their argument makes any real difference. If the seller has no money, the buyer keeps the ox anyway, so they must argue where the seller can repay. רב says the sale is a מקח טעות because we follow רוב, and most people buy oxen for plowing. שמואל answers that we follow רוב only in איסורא, not in ממונא. A סימן then lists five cases that will test these views. First, a משנה about a כתובה seems to show that רוב does not decide money cases, but רבינא explains that the majority there is weakened because her wedding had no publicity. That answer is sharpened to say that most virgin weddings, not all, are publicized. The גמרא then quotes a ברייתא about a sold slave with defects to challenge שמואל, and begins explaining it at the end of the amud, with the argument continuing on the next amud.

steps.title: If the seller cannot pay, the buyer keeps the ox anyway
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: if the seller has no money to return, the buyer will hold on to the ox as payment. So even by רב there would be no practical change.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the seller has nothing to repay the buyer with, then the buyer should just keep the ox in place of his money. As people say: from someone who owes you, collect even bran.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is pushing back on a possible case of the רב–שמואל argument. It says that in this case the argument would not change anything.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under רב the sale is cancelled and the buyer should get his money back. But if the seller is broke, the buyer will simply keep the ox as his payment, which is the same result as under שמואל. So this cannot be the case where their argument really matters.

keyTerms.meaning: let him hold on to / keep
bran, a cheap leftover grain product

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a question about the law of the ox itself. The גמרא is only searching for a case where רב and שמואל would actually end up with different results.

phrases.english: If there is nothing to be repaid from him,
let the buyer hold on to the ox in place of his money!
As people say:
From the one who owes you, collect even bran!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי דְּלֵיכָּא לְאִישְׁתַּלּוֹמֵי מִינֵּיהּ, לִיעַכַּב תּוֹרָא בְּזוּזֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier search on this daf for the practical case behind the רב–שמואל dispute.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that רב and שמואל argue in a case where the seller cannot repay.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the seller cannot repay, the buyer keeps the ox even under רב, so the two opinions lead to the same result.

steps.title: They argue where the seller is able to repay
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the dispute is needed for a case where the seller does have money to return.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the argument is needed for the case where the seller does have the money to repay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the objection by moving the case. Now the seller has money, so cancelling the sale really matters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the seller can pay, רב's ruling of מקח טעות gives the buyer back his cash instead of a goring ox. שמואל's ruling leaves him stuck with the ox. Now the two opinions truly lead to different results.

keyTerms.meaning: no, it is needed for (a specific case)

phrases.english: No, it is needed for where there is money to be repaid from him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the objection in step 1.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Their argument might apply even when the seller is broke, where it would make no difference.
steps.terutzMaskana: The argument applies when the seller can repay, so cancelling the sale means real money changes hands.

steps.title: רב's reasoning: follow the majority, who buy for plowing
steps.stepSummary: רב rules the sale is a מקח טעות because we follow רוב, and most people buy oxen for plowing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: This is a mistaken sale. We go after the majority, and most people buy oxen for plowing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now explains the logic behind רב's opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We do not know why this buyer bought the ox. רב settles the doubt by looking at what most buyers do. Most buy oxen to plow, so we assume this buyer did too. A goring ox is unfit for plowing, so the sale was based on a mistake.

keyTerms.meaning: a mistaken sale, which is cancelled

phrases.aramaic: רַב אָמַר: הֲרֵי זֶה מִקָּח טָעוּת –
phrases.english: Rav said: This is a mistaken sale –
we go after the majority,
and the majority buy oxen for plowing.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָמַר: הֲרֵי זֶה מִקָּח טָעוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: With the case now set, the גמרא explains רב's side.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The sale is cancelled, because we assume the buyer is like most buyers, who buy oxen for plowing.

steps.title: שמואל's reply: majority applies only in ritual law, not money
steps.stepSummary: שמואל would answer that we follow רוב only in איסורא (ritual law), not in ממונא (money matters).
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל would say to you: When we go after the majority, that is in ritual law. In money matters we do not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives שמואל's answer to רב's reasoning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל agrees that רוב is a real rule, but he limits where it applies. In money cases we do not use the majority to take money away from someone. So there is no basis to cancel the sale, and the seller keeps the payment.

keyTerms.meaning: ritual law, matters of permitted and forbidden

steps.whatToRemember: רב: follow רוב even in money, so most buyers buy for plowing and the sale is a מקח טעות. שמואל: אין הולכין אחר הרוב בממון, so the sale stands.
steps.whyThisMatters: The question of whether רוב is used in money cases is a basic principle across ש״ס. The coming cases are meant to test it.

phrases.english: And Shmuel would say to you:
When we go after the majority – that is in ritual law,
in money matters – no.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר לָךְ: כִּי אָזְלִינַן בָּתַר רוּבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to רב's reasoning by limiting where רוב applies.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects using רוב in this money case, without rejecting רוב in general.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רב applied the majority rule to a money case, but שמואל holds that it works only for ritual law.

steps.title: Memory aid for the five upcoming cases
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a סימן listing the topics it will use next to challenge רב or שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: A memory aid: woman, and slave, ox, oxen, and produce.
steps.whatsHappening: This line sets up the next part of the גמרא. It lists, in order, the five cases that are about to be brought as challenges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word stands for an upcoming case about following the majority in money matters. The list does not teach any law. It only helps the learner remember the order of the challenges.

phrases.english: (Memory aid: woman, and slave,
ox, oxen, and produce.)

steps.triggerLanguage: סִימָן: אִשָּׁה, וְעֶבֶד, שׁוֹר, שְׁוָרִין, וּפֵירוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After both sides are explained, this line prepares a series of challenges to them.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling. It only lists the order of the coming cases.

steps.title: Quoting a משנה about a disputed כתובה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a משנה: a widowed or divorced woman says she married as a virgin and he says she was a widow. If witnesses saw her wedding done in the virgin style, her כתובה is 200.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged רב from this: A woman was widowed or divorced. She says, 'I was a virgin when I married,' and he says, 'No, you were a widow when I married you.' If there are witnesses that she went out to her wedding with a הינומא and with her hair loose, her כתובה is 200.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting a משנה to set up a challenge against רב. The challenge itself comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A virgin's כתובה is 200 and a widow's is 100, so the couple is arguing about money. In this case the משנה rules for the woman because there are witnesses. The גמרא will now ask why she needs witnesses at all.

keyTerms.meaning: A special veil or canopy used at a virgin's wedding.
Her hair loose and uncovered, a sign of a virgin bride.
Her כתובה is 200 זוז, the amount for a virgin.

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
phrases.notes: The source is a משנה in כתובות. It is being used against רב.

phrases.english: A woman who was widowed or divorced,
and she says: I married as a virgin,
and he says: Not so,
rather, I married you as a widow.
If there are witnesses that she went out with a veil,
phrases.notes: She went out from her father's house to the wedding.

phrases.english: and with her hair loose,
her marriage contract is two hundred.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is the first of the challenges listed in the סימן in step 5. It brings a source to test רב's rule that we follow רוב in money cases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If witnesses saw a virgin-style wedding, the woman collects a כתובה of 200.

steps.title: Why does she need witnesses if most women marry as virgins?
steps.stepSummary: The משנה suggests that without witnesses she would not get 200. But if we follow רוב, she should get 200 anyway, since most women marry as virgins. So it seems we do not follow רוב in money cases, which goes against רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason she gets 200 is that there are witnesses. Without witnesses she would not. But why not? Let us say we follow the majority of women, and most women marry as virgins!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads a hidden point out of the משנה and uses it to attack רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the משנה needs witnesses, she would lose without them. If רוב worked in money matters, the majority alone should win the case for her. This seems to back שמואל's view that we do not follow רוב in ממונא.

keyTerms.meaning: The reason; it introduces a reading of what a source implies.
But if there is not; this shows the opposite case.

phrases.english: The reason is that there are witnesses,
but if there are no witnesses, no.
phrases.notes: He means she would not get 200 without witnesses.

phrases.english: But why?
Let us say: follow the majority of women,
and most women marry as virgins!

steps.triggerLanguage: טַעְמָא דְּאִיכָּא עֵדִים, הָא לֵיכָּא עֵדִים – לָא; וְאַמַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It reads a point out of the משנה quoted in step 6 and turns it into a challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that we follow רוב in money matters.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה needs witnesses in a money case, even though the majority (most women marry as virgins) is on her side. So the majority alone is not enough in ממונא.

steps.title: רבינא: Her missing publicity weakens the majority
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers that most women do marry as virgins, but a virgin's wedding is always well known. Since nobody heard about her wedding being a virgin's wedding, the majority no longer helps her.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: It is because you can say this. Most women marry as virgins and a minority as widows. But every woman who marries as a virgin gets a 'voice' (it becomes well known). This woman has no such voice, so the majority is weakened for her.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא defends רב. He explains why the majority does not decide this case, even if we do follow רוב in money matters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא does not say that רוב fails in money cases. He says this particular majority is weakened by another fact: virgin weddings are normally public, and hers was not. So the משנה is no proof against רב.

keyTerms.meaning: She has a 'voice'; her virgin wedding becomes well known.
The majority is weakened for her.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
It is because one can say:
most women marry as virgins,
and a minority as widows;

phrases.aramaic: וְכׇל הַנִּישֵּׂאת בְּתוּלָה – יֵשׁ לָהּ קוֹל;
phrases.english: but every woman who marries as a virgin has publicity;
and this one, since she has no publicity,
the majority is weakened for her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It answers the challenge in step 7 and saves רב's position.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A competing fact weakens the majority in this specific case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Needing witnesses shows that רוב does not work in money cases.
steps.terutzMaskana: רוב can still work in money cases. Here it is weakened because she lacks the publicity that virgin weddings normally have.
steps.confusionAlert: רבינא does not deny that most women marry as virgins. He only says that this majority stops helping in her case, because her wedding was not well known.

steps.title: If virgin weddings are always known, her witnesses must be lying
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא attacks רבינא: if every virgin wedding is publicized, then hers was not one. Any witnesses who say otherwise should be treated as false witnesses, so why does the משנה trust them?
steps.simpleTranslation: If every woman who marries as a virgin has publicity, what difference do witnesses make? Since she has no publicity, they must be false witnesses!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבינא's answer by following his idea all the way through.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא treated 'every virgin wedding is known' as a strong rule. If it is that strong, the lack of publicity should prove she was not a virgin bride. Then her witnesses would be liars, but the משנה accepts them.

phrases.aramaic: אִי כׇּל הַנִּישָּׂאוֹת בְּתוּלוֹת יֵשׁ לָהֶן קוֹל,
phrases.english: If all who marry as virgins have publicity,
when there are witnesses, what of it?
Since she has no publicity,
they are false witnesses!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי כׇּל הַנִּישָּׂאוֹת בְּתוּלוֹת יֵשׁ לָהֶן קוֹל, כִּי אִיכָּא עֵדִים מַאי הָוֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It challenges רבינא's answer from step 8 by showing it clashes with the משנה in step 6, which trusts the witnesses.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבינא's claim that every virgin wedding has publicity.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If publicity always comes with a virgin wedding, then no publicity proves she was not a virgin bride. Her witnesses would then be lying, yet the משנה accepts them.

steps.title: Most virgin weddings are publicized, so no publicity weakens the majority
steps.stepSummary: The answer is reworded: most virgin weddings have publicity, not all of them. Since her wedding had none, the רוב is weakened for her, but witnesses can still be believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say it this way: most women who marry as virgins have publicity about it. This woman had no publicity, so the majority no longer helps her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes רבינא's answer so it no longer runs into the problem raised in Step 9.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 9 the trouble came from saying every virgin wedding is publicized, because then witnesses who say she had one would have to be lying. Now the claim is only that most virgin weddings are publicized. So her missing publicity weakens the רוב, which is why she cannot claim 200 on her own. But she could still be one of the few virgins whose wedding was quiet, which is why witnesses are believed.
steps.whatToRemember: Missing publicity does not erase the majority. It only weakens it enough that she needs witnesses. This keeps the משנה consistent with רב, who says we follow רוב in money cases.
steps.confusionAlert: The change is only one word in meaning: from 'every' virgin wedding has publicity to 'most' do. That small change is what lets the witnesses be believed.

phrases.english: Rather, most women who marry as virgins
have publicity,
and this one, since she has no publicity,
the majority is weakened for her.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא רוֹב הַנִּישָּׂאוֹת בְּתוּלוֹת יֵשׁ לָהֶן קוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the attack in Step 9 by rewording רבינא's answer from Step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rewording the earlier answer so it claims less
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every virgin wedding is publicized, so witnesses who say she had one would have to be false.
steps.terutzMaskana: Most virgin weddings are publicized. Lack of publicity weakens the רוב but leaves room for witnesses to be believed.

steps.title: A ברייתא about selling a slave who turns out to have a defect
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא to challenge שמואל. If a sold slave turns out to be a thief or gambler, the sale stands. If he turns out to be an armed bandit or condemned by the government, the buyer can return him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if someone sells a slave to another person and the slave turns out to be a thief or a gambler, the buyer keeps him. If he turns out to be an armed bandit or someone the government has sentenced, the buyer can say to the seller: 'Here is your slave back.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new challenge, this time against שמואל, by quoting a ברייתא. The actual argument from it comes in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל says we do not follow רוב in money cases. The ברייתא gives two clauses: small defects that do not undo the sale, and serious ones that do. The גמרא will read these clauses closely to find something that clashes with שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: A gambler, such as someone who plays dice
It has come to him: the buyer is stuck with the sale
Written up by the government: sentenced to death by the authorities

steps.whyThisMatters: After defending רב, the גמרא now turns to test שמואל, so both sides of the debate get challenged.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
One who sells a slave to his fellow
and he turns out to be a thief or a gambler,
it has come to him.
phrases.notes: He means the buyer keeps the slave and cannot cancel the sale.

phrases.english: An armed bandit, or one written up for the government:
he says to him: Here is yours before you.
phrases.notes: In other words, 'Take your slave back and give me my money.' The sale is cancelled.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from defending רב to bringing a source that challenges שמואל, following the list of topics given in Step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's view that we do not follow רוב in money cases
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא's ruling on which defects cancel a sale will be shown to clash with שמואל. The full argument comes next.

steps.title: Starting to explain the first clause
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to break down the first clause of the ברייתא to build its challenge against שמואל.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא points to the first clause of the ברייתא (the thief or gambler) and is about to explain what it proves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before attacking, the גמרא goes through the ברייתא one clause at a time. The thought that starts here is finished on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: The first clause of a משנה or ברייתא
The later clause; the pair to רֵישָׁא
A teaching of the תנאים that was left out of the משנה

phrases.english: The first clause:
phrases.notes: This means the thief or gambler case. The sentence continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts drawing an inference from the ברייתא quoted in Step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's view that we do not follow רוב in money cases
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The argument is only just starting; it will be built from reading the first clause closely.
